title: Behavioral Detection of Mailbox Data and Log Deletion for Anti-Forensics
shortTitle: Behavioral Detection of Mailbox Data and Log Deletion for...
summary: This detection strategy covers deletion of mailbox data and related records as an anti-forensics step, tracked as T1070.008. An adversary who has mailbox permissions, or an administrator account, can remove both the messages and the audit trail that would prove what happened. Detection depends on the mail platform audit log itself, which records hard delete and purge operations along with changes to audit settings, plus administrative activity that disables auditing or weakens retention. The strategy fails when auditing is already disabled on the mailbox, when the deletion is performed by a scheduled retention policy, and when the audit records are stored in the same tenant the intruder controls.

beginner.definition: A mailbox holds a person's email. Mail platforms keep a record of actions taken on messages, called an audit log. Anti-forensics means removing evidence after an intrusion. This detection looks for actions that delete mail in bulk and for changes that turn the mail audit log off.
beginner.whyItMatters: Email often holds the proof of a fraud, a phishing campaign, or a data transfer. An intruder who deletes those messages removes the evidence before anyone looks. Worse, turning off the audit log hides the deletion itself. This makes the technique a direct attack on your ability to investigate. Detecting the removal, and the change to auditing, protects the rest of your case.
howItWorks: The mail platform writes an audit entry for each message operation, including who did it.
Those entries are copied to a central store that the mail administrator cannot change.
The rule counts delete and purge operations per account over a short window.
A second rule watches for changes that disable auditing or extend retention limits.
Deletions that follow an administrator sign-in from a new location add weight to the alert.
Analysts receive both the operation list and the account that made the changes.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop that keeps a paper receipt for every sale. A cashier who wants to hide a theft has two jobs. First, remove the receipts. Second, switch off the till's printing. A good owner notices both events. The missing receipts alone might be an error, but turning off the printer is deliberate. Mailbox deletion and audit tampering are the same pair.
takeaways: Deleting mailbox data and disabling mailbox auditing are two halves of one technique.
Store audit records somewhere the mail administrator cannot reach.
A sudden burst of deletions by one account is the clearest signal.

objectives: Explain why mailbox data is both evidence and a target
Collect mail platform audit logs into tamper resistant storage
Detect bulk delete and purge operations per account
Alert on changes that disable mailbox auditing or weaken retention
Correlate deletion bursts with administrative sign-in anomalies
dataSources: Mail platform mailbox audit logs recording hard delete, soft delete, and move to deleted items operations with the acting user
Mail server administrative audit records for audit bypass settings and retention policy changes
Cloud collaboration audit logs for permanent purge operations and for disabling mailbox auditing
Identity provider sign-in logs for the administrative account that performed the mailbox operations
Mail gateway message tracking logs showing the original delivery that is later missing
logic: The pattern is a mailbox losing items at an unusual rate, or the controls that record such changes being switched off. The rule aggregates mail platform audit entries by acting account and operation type, counting hard deletes, purges, and moves to deleted items over a rolling window, and separately selects configuration operations that disable mailbox auditing or remove retention and hold settings. The malicious case usually combines a burst of deletions with a recent administrative sign-in from an unusual address, or with the audit setting change itself, while legitimate cases are single message deletions by their owner, retention policies applied on schedule by the platform, and hold changes made through a documented legal case. Correlating the two operation families is what separates housekeeping from evidence removal.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk mailbox item deletion combined with a mailbox audit change
# logsource:
#   product: azure
# detection:
#   selection_delete:
#     event_type: 'mailbox_item'
#     operation|contains:
#       - 'HardDelete'
#       - 'SoftDelete'
#       - 'MoveToDeletedItems'
#   selection_audit:
#     operation|contains: 'AuditBypassAssociation'
#   filter:
#     actor: 'retention-policy-service'
#   condition: (selection_delete or selection_audit) and not filter
# level: high
falsePositives: A retention policy that removes messages older than the agreed period on a nightly schedule
A user who empties a large folder after a mailbox cleanup request from the helpdesk
A legal or compliance team that releases a hold after a case is closed
Migration tooling that deletes the source copy after a successful mailbox move
tuningNotes: Exclude the platform retention service identity and any documented migration tool, and set a volume threshold that sits above normal user housekeeping, measured per mailbox rather than per tenant. Keep the audit configuration changes at high severity with no threshold, because disabling auditing is never routine. Baseline who normally changes retention and hold settings in your organisation, so that a single unexpected actor stands out. Narrowing by threshold loses coverage for a careful intruder who deletes a small number of critical messages, so review deletions of messages that are under legal hold as a separate rule.
